weaknesses: Proposition 3 has a substantive finite-sample gap. Standard CP applied to the transformed score guarantees coverage for {Fhat_y(s) <= q}, whereas Raw FUZZY at quantile level q uses {Fhat_y(s) < q}. Because the empirical transformation creates atoms, these sets are not equivalent. With equal weights, independent continuous scores, n=1, m=9, and alpha=0.1, the literal quantile-level prescription yields coverage 9/22 rather than at least 0.9. The implementation needs explicit tie handling and a corrected proof; exchangeability alone does not establish the stated result.

The experimental protocol does not satisfy the assumptions underlying the coverage guarantees. Appendix B.2 explicitly reuses validation data for both checkpoint selection and conformal calibration. Comparing one validation quantile with its test counterpart does not establish that this reuse is harmless. Evaluation with an independent calibration split is necessary.

Statistical reliability is insufficiently established. The main trade-off curves lack uncertainty estimates across calibration splits or random seeds, despite sparse tail-class test samples and randomized class mappings. The truncated datasets improve measurement precision but retain only 330/1,081 and 857/8,142 classes, leaving uncertainty about performance across the original tails.

Important comparisons are missing, particularly the rank-calibrated class-conditional method of Shi et al. (2024), which the introduction discusses but does not evaluate. All experiments also use one ResNet-50 training recipe. Comparisons with prior-adjusted scoring and stronger long-tailed classifiers would better establish the contribution beyond familiar prevalence correction and kernel pooling.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence. PAS optimality is established with oracle probabilities, without an estimation-error analysis supporting approximate optimality for learned probabilities. The recommendation to generally avoid CLASSWISE also overlooks its stronger per-class guarantee, which the proposed methods relinquish. The simulated human analysis illustrates stipulated decision rules rather than independently validating human utility.

Reproducibility is incomplete: Section 3 announces available code but provides no link, and training details omit items such as optimizer, batch size, and augmentation. Exact implementation details are especially important given the quantile-boundary issue.

strengths: Addresses an important practical failure of conformal prediction: small marginally valid sets can systematically exclude rare classes. The distinction between marginal, macro, and class-conditional coverage is clear and useful.

The oracle characterization provides a principled motivation for PAS and its weighted extension. Both are simple to implement and retain standard split-conformal marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability.

The empirical improvements are meaningful. On Pl@ntNet, PAS increases macro-coverage from 0.525 to 0.755 and reduces the fraction of classes with empirical coverage at most 50% from 0.389 to 0.167, while increasing average set size from 1.57 to 2.57 and maintaining approximately 90% marginal coverage. iNaturalist also shows improvements, although smaller.

The evaluation includes two large long-tailed datasets, several coverage levels, standard/classwise/clustered baselines, a randomized classwise baseline, focal-loss experiments, and truncated datasets for more reliable classwise evaluation. The appendix provides substantial supporting analysis.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: the oracle result specializes Neyman–Pearson reasoning, PAS applies inverse-prevalence weighting, and INTERP-Q linearly shrinks thresholds. Comparisons with conformal prediction using logit-adjusted classifiers and the cited rank-calibrated method would better establish the contribution beyond existing approaches.

The optimality result concerns true population probabilities. It does not establish approximate optimality for the learned PAS score, whose calibration guarantees marginal coverage rather than a specified macro-coverage level. The broad empirical claim of Pareto optimality in Section 3.1 should be restricted to the evaluated methods and settings.

INTERP-Q guarantees only 1−2α marginal coverage, whereas STANDARD and PAS guarantee 1−α. Empirical coverage near 1−α does not eliminate this distinction. Comparisons at matched guaranteed coverage would strengthen the case, and recommending that CLASSWISE generally be avoided overlooks its stronger class-conditional guarantee.

Experimental robustness remains insufficiently characterized: results use one architecture, two related biodiversity datasets, and no reported repeated-run uncertainty or confidence intervals. Rare-class threshold metrics are particularly noisy with tiny test samples; the truncated experiments help but exclude many of the hardest tail classes.

Proposition 7 needs stronger kernel assumptions. Off-diagonal weights tending to zero does not imply that they vanish relative to self-weights, which is needed for the claimed CLASSWISE limit. Normalized-weight convergence conditions would repair this auxiliary result.
